Kenneth Craik

Kenneth Craik (1914–1945) may have been the first thinker to state the central thesis of this book in explicit terms. In The Nature of Explanation 1, he proposed that the brain constructs “small-scale models” of external reality that it uses to try out alternatives, anticipate events, and select among possible actions. “If the organism carries a ‘small-scale model’ of external reality and of its own possible actions within its head, it is able to try out various alternatives, conclude which is the best of them, react to future situations before they arise.” Craik died in a cycling accident at thirty-one; his vision would take decades to be realized in computational form.

Alan Turing

Alan Turing (1912–1954) provided the formal foundation for any computational theory of the brain. His 1936 paper 2 showed that a simple abstract machine (the Turing machine) can compute anything that is computable. In “Computing Machinery and Intelligence” 3, he posed the question of whether machines can think and proposed the imitation game (Turing test) as a pragmatic criterion. The question that computational neuroscience inherits from Turing is precise: what does the brain compute, and how?

Maurice Merleau-Ponty

Maurice Merleau-Ponty (1908–1961) mounted the most influential philosophical challenge to disembodied, representationalist accounts of the mind 4, 5. Perception is not the brain’s construction of an internal replica; it is the body’s active engagement with the world. The body schema—a pre-reflective, motor understanding of the body’s capabilities and position—is the medium through which the world shows up as meaningful. Pathological cases (phantom limbs, spatial neglect, apraxia) reveal that perception and action are inseparable. His work is the primary philosophical source for the embodied cognition movement and remains a standing challenge to purely internalist world-modeling accounts.

Gilbert Ryle

Gilbert Ryle (1900–1976) attacked Cartesian dualism in The Concept of Mind 6 as a “category mistake”—the error of treating the mind as a “ghost in the machine,” a hidden inner theater where experience is privately screened. Mental predicates (knowing, believing, intending) are not reports of inner episodes but descriptions of dispositions to behave in certain ways. Though few neuroscientists accept full-blown behaviorism, Ryle’s critique sharpened the question: what explanatory work does an “internal model” do that cannot be captured by the organism’s dispositions to act?

Wilfrid Sellars

Wilfrid Sellars (1912–1989) demolished the Myth of the Given in “Empiricism and the Philosophy of Mind” 7: there is no level of experience that is simply “given” to the mind, raw and uninterpreted. All perceptual experience is already theory-laden—structured by concepts, expectations, and inferential commitments. His distinction between the manifest image (the world as it appears to everyday experience) and the scientific image (the world as described by physics and neuroscience) defines the central tension of the field: the brain’s world model produces the manifest image, but the scientific image tells us that the manifest image is a construction of neural processes that are nothing like how the world appears.

Norbert Wiener

Norbert Wiener (1894–1964) named and defined the field of cybernetics: the study of “control and communication in the animal and the machine” 8. The foundational insight is that organisms and engineered systems share a common architecture of negative feedback: a system continuously compares its current state to a reference state and acts to minimize the discrepancy. Purposive behavior, on this view, is not metaphysically mysterious; it is any behavior governed by feedback toward a set-point. Wiener’s framework—in which the brain is a self-regulating, stochastic, information-processing system that acts to minimize the divergence between expected and actual states—is a direct intellectual ancestor of the free energy principle’s account of action as the minimization of prediction error.

W. Ross Ashby

W. Ross Ashby (1903–1972) asked, more precisely than anyone before him, what it takes for a physical system to be genuinely adaptive 9, 10. His homeostat—an electromechanical device with randomly connected feedback loops that settles, through a process of trial and ultra-stability, into configurations maintaining essential variables within survival-compatible bounds—was a physical proof of concept that self-organizing, adaptive behavior requires neither a designer nor explicit goal representations. His law of requisite variety states that a regulator must possess at least as many distinguishable internal states as the system it controls—a formal lower bound on the complexity of any viable world model. In the idiom of the free energy principle, the brain’s generative model must be rich enough to account for the variability of its sensory input; Ashby’s law specifies the minimum complexity this demands.
